items.title: Why try/catch misses a promise you did not await
items.body:
The key is right: without `await`, the `try` block finishes before the promise rejects, so the rejection is never caught there. Calling an async function starts it and immediately returns a promise. The `try` only watches code that runs inside it, and nothing inside it is waiting. When the promise later rejects, the `catch` is long gone and the rejection is unhandled. The module's key points say it in one line: try/catch around `await` works, around a non-awaited promise it does not. The fix is `await saveUser(user)` or a `.catch(...)` on the promise.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Async functions cannot throw**: a throw inside an async function becomes a rejected promise; it does reject.
- **Logged after timers drain**: nothing ever routes the rejection to that `catch`, at any time.
- **catch only runs for engine errors**: with `await`, `catch` does receive async rejections.

excerpts.quote: "try/catch around await works; try/catch around a non-awaited promise does not"
"An async function always returns a promise, even if you return a plain value",

items.title: Why Promise.all rejects at once but cannot stop the others
items.body:
The key is right: the other nine requests keep running, but the caller's `await` rejects as soon as the first one fails. The module's model answer says `Promise.all` rejects as soon as any input rejects, and "the others keep running, you just don't get their values." JavaScript promises have no built-in cancel button, so a rejection cannot stop work that has already started. If you need every outcome, the key points name `allSettled` instead.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Waits for all ten, error in slot three**: that is closer to what `allSettled` does (it reports an outcome per slot). `Promise.all` does not wait.
- **Cancelled automatically**: promises are not cancellable; the model answer says the others keep running.
- **Rejection swallowed, nine values returned**: `Promise.all` rejects; it never hands back a partial array.

excerpts.quote: "Promise.all rejects on the first failure; allSettled always resolves with the outcomes",
`Promise.all` resolves with an array of all results, but rejects as soon as *any* input rejects — the others keep running, you just don't get their values.

items.title: Why 'thistle' counts as the keyword 'this'
items.body:
The key is right: yes, it counts, because only the left boundary is enforced. `keywordScore` pads the text with spaces and then accepts a keyword if the haystack contains it with a space on both sides OR with just a space before it. The second test only needs the leading space. " thistle" contains " this", so the keyword is marked as a hit. The doc comment claims word boundaries stop "this" matching inside "something". That works only because "something" has letters before "this"; nothing checks the right side.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Ignores spaces, searches anywhere**: both tests require a leading space, so "something" would not match.
- **Both sides wrapped, whole word only**: that is the first test, but the second test (no trailing space) also counts.
- **Trailing letters stripped**: the code only replaces characters outside `[a-z0-9+#.\s-]` with spaces; letters are kept.

const haystack = ` ${text.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9+#.\s-]/g, " ").replace(/\s+/g, " ")} `;
const found = alternatives.some((alt) => haystack.includes(` ${alt} `) || haystack.includes(` ${alt}`));

items.title: Why a slow correct answer is rated Hard
items.body:
The key is right: rating 2 (Hard). `ratingFor` checks in order: incorrect gives 1, partial gives 2, a used hint gives 2, then `timeSpent > estSeconds * 2` gives 2. With an estimate of 30 seconds, the limit is 60; 70 seconds is over it, so the function returns 2 before it ever reaches the Easy or Good lines. The doc comment gives the reason: speed matters for interview recall, and an answer you had to think about for a minute is not one you "know".

Why the others are wrong:
- **1 (Again)**: 1 is returned only for an "incorrect" verdict; this answer was correct.
- **3 (Good) whatever the time**: the time check runs before the final `return 3`, so time does change the rating.
- **4 (Easy)**: Easy needs `timeSpent < estSeconds * 0.5` (under 15 seconds here).

excerpts.quote: /** * Turn a grade into a review rating. Speed matters for interview recall — an * answer you had to think about for a minute is not one you "know".

if (grade.verdict === "incorrect") return 1; if (grade.verdict === "partial") return 2; if (usedHint) return 2; if (timeSpent > estSeconds * 2) return 2; if (timeSpent < estSeconds * 0.5) return 4; return 3;

items.title: Why runCode starts a fresh worker every run
items.body:
The key is right: a runaway loop can be killed after the 3 s timeout, and each run gets a clean global scope. The doc comment on `runCode` gives exactly these two reasons: terminating the worker is the only way to interrupt a runaway loop, and a new worker means a previous attempt can't leak state into this one. The code backs it up: a `setTimeout` of `TIMEOUT_MS` (3000) calls `worker.terminate()` and fails every test with error type "timeout".

Why the others are wrong:
- **Workers start faster, console hidden**: starting a worker is extra work, not a speed-up, and the comment says nothing about hiding output.
- **Server event loop, worker reads the database**: the worker is `/sandbox.js`, the file in `public/`, and it is sent only the code, test cases and entry point.
- **Parallel tests, cached compilation**: one worker runs one submission and is then terminated, so nothing is cached between runs.

excerpts.quote: * The worker is spawned per run and terminated afterwards: it's the only way * to interrupt a runaway loop, and it also guarantees each run starts from a * clean global scope so a previous attempt can't leak state into this one.

items.title: Why ticking every box scores zero on a multi item
items.body:
The key is right: score 0, verdict incorrect. `gradeMulti` counts `hit` (picked and correct) and `wrong` (picked but not correct), then computes `Math.max(0, (hit - wrong) / correct.size)`. Ticking all four boxes with correct set {A, C} gives hit = 2 and wrong = 2, so (2 - 2) / 2 = 0. `verdictFor` maps a score of 0 to "incorrect". The comment says it plainly: reward hits, punish false positives equally. That is what makes select-all worthless.

Why the others are wrong:
- **2 / 4 = 0.5**: the divisor is `correct.size` (2), not the number of choices, and wrong picks are subtracted.
- **Half the ticks are right, half credit**: wrong picks cancel hits; they do not just dilute them.
- **Score 1, extras ignored**: extras are counted as `wrong` and subtracted.

excerpts.quote: // Jaccard-style credit: reward hits, punish false positives equally. let hit = 0; let wrong = 0; for (const i of picked) { if (correct.has(i)) hit++; else wrong++; } const missed = correct.size - hit; const score = correct.size === 0 ? 0 : Math.max(0, (hit - wrong) / correct.size);
function verdictFor(score: number): Verdict { if (score >= 0.999) return "correct"; if (score > 0) return "partial"; return "incorrect";

items.title: How mastery fades while a card is overdue
items.body:
The key is right: mastery fades linearly over twice the stability (20 days here) and never drops below 0.35 of its value. In `cardMastery`, once `overdueDays > 0`, the code sets `window = Math.max(row.stability, 1) * 2` and multiplies mastery by `Math.max(0.35, 1 - overdueDays / window)`. With stability 10, the window is 20 days. Each overdue day takes off 1/20 of the value, in a straight line, until the 0.35 floor stops it. The comment explains the floor: you haven't forgotten it completely, you're just due.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Halves every interval toward zero**: the formula is a straight line with a floor, not repeated halving, and it never reaches zero.
- **Drops straight to zero when due**: the multiplier starts near 1 and has a 0.35 floor.
- **Stays until the next review**: `cardMastery` reads the current time `at`, so mastery changes with no review at all.

excerpts.quote: const overdueDays = (at.getTime() - new Date(row.due).getTime()) / 86_400_000; if (overdueDays > 0) { // Fade over roughly twice the interval the card had earned, and never all // the way to zero — you haven't forgotten it completely, you're just due. const window = Math.max(row.stability, 1) * 2; mastery *= Math.max(0.35, 1 - overdueDays / window); }

items.title: Why one correct answer shows about 46% mastery
items.body:
The key is right: about 46%. In `cardMastery`, a card with at least one rep and not in Relearning gets `floor = 0.4`. Then `retention = Math.min(row.stability, 30) / 30`, which is 3 / 30 = 0.1, and `mastery = floor + retention * (1 - floor)` = 0.4 + 0.1 x 0.6 = 0.46. It is not overdue, so no fade applies. The comment explains why it is not higher: stability only grows through successful reviews, so the top of the range has to be earned over time rather than in one sitting.

Why the others are wrong:
- **100%, correct and not due**: being correct earns only the floor plus stability's share.
- **10%, stability / 30 with no floor**: the 0.4 floor is added on top.
- **0% until it leaves learning**: the code returns 0 only when `reps === 0`; after one review reps is 1.

excerpts.quote: if (row.reps === 0) return 0; // A lapsed card is back in relearning — treat it as barely known again. const floor = row.state === State.Relearning ? 0.15 : 0.4; const retention = Math.min(row.stability, 30) / 30; let mastery = floor + retention * (1 - floor);

items.title: Why two of four steps in place scores 0.25
items.body:
The key is right: 0.25, because positional credit is squared. `gradeOrder` counts how many positions match (`hit`), computes `raw = hit / expected.length`, and then `score = raw >= 1 ? 1 : raw * raw`. Two of four in place is raw 0.5, and 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25, which `verdictFor` calls partial. The comment gives the reason: all-or-nothing feels harsh, but a half-right pipeline is still wrong in production, so credit is weighted quadratically.

Why the others are wrong:
- **0.75 for relative order**: the code only compares each position (`response.order[i] === exp`); relative order earns nothing.
- **0.5, one point per step**: that is `raw` before squaring; the returned score is squared.
- **0, all-or-nothing**: the comment explicitly rejects all-or-nothing, and partial answers score above 0.

excerpts.quote: const detail = expected.map((exp, i) => response.order[i] === exp); const hit = detail.filter(Boolean).length; // All-or-nothing feels harsh, but a half-right pipeline is still wrong in // production, so weight positional credit quadratically. const raw = expected.length === 0 ? 0 : hit / expected.length; const score = raw >= 1 ? 1 : raw * raw;

items.title: What request_retention 0.88 trades away
items.body:
The key is right: slightly longer intervals and a bit more forgetting, in exchange for covering more distinct material. `request_retention` is the recall chance the scheduler aims for when it next shows a card. Aiming a little lower (0.88 instead of the default 0.9) lets it wait longer between reviews, which frees time for other cards. The comment says why: interview prep is broad, and seeing more distinct material beats drilling the same card to perfection.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Shorter intervals, drilled to perfection**: that is the opposite direction; the comment says this setting avoids drilling to perfection.
- **Disables fuzzing**: the same line sets `enable_fuzz: true`, so fuzzing is on.
- **Deterministic for tests**: with fuzz enabled, due dates are deliberately not exact; the comment gives a learning reason, not a testing one.

excerpts.quote: /** * Slightly lower retention than the default 0.9: interview prep is broad, and * seeing more distinct material beats drilling the same card to perfection. */ const scheduler = fsrs(generatorParameters({ request_retention: 0.88, enable_fuzz: true }));

items.title: Why reordering questions breaks review history
items.body:
The key is right: the reordered items get new ids, so their stored review history no longer lines up with the questions. The README says ids come from the track slug, module slug and **position**. Editing an explanation or appending a question at the end keeps every existing position, so schedules survive. Moving question 5 to the top shifts the position of every question it passes, and the README warns that reordering or removing items changes ids.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Seed refuses until a version bump**: the README describes no version check; `db:seed` is an upsert it calls "safe to re-run".
- **Ids are hashes of the prompt text**: the README says position, not prompt text.
- **Only the moved item loses history**: every item whose position changes gets a new id, not just the one you moved.

excerpts.quote: Item ids are derived from the track slug, module slug and position, so editing an explanation or appending a question leaves everyone's review schedule intact. **Reordering or removing items changes ids**, and removed items take their review history with them.

items.title: Start here: how Ramp turns your answers into a schedule
items.body:
Ramp is a local interview-practice app. You answer questions, a grader scores each answer, and a scheduler decides when you see that question again. This pack quizzes you on that machinery, plus two lessons from the JavaScript question bank.

Suggested reading order:

1. **README.md**, top to "How it works". It names the seven question formats and says where each part of the app lives.
2. **README.md, "Project layout"**. Note the three files that matter most here: `grading.ts` (scores every format and picks the review rating), `fsrs.ts` (scheduling and the mastery curve) and `executor.ts` (talks to the code sandbox).
3. **src/lib/grading.ts**. Read one grader function per format. Each one is short and starts with a banner comment naming the format.
4. **src/lib/fsrs.ts**, the `cardMastery` function and the comment above it.
5. **src/lib/executor.ts**, the doc comment on `runCode`.
6. **README.md, "Adding questions"**, for how question ids are made.
7. **seed-data/content/javascript.json**, the `async-javascript` module's `keyPoints`.

Tip: when a quiz asks "what score", find the line that computes `score` and do the arithmetic by hand with the numbers in the prompt.

items.title: Core idea: each question format has its own grader
items.body:
Ramp has seven formats (`mcq`, `multi`, `predict`, `fill`, `order`, `code`, `explain`) and `grading.ts` has one function per format. Every grader returns a `score` between 0 and 1. A shared helper, `verdictFor`, turns that number into a word: a score of at least 0.999 is "correct", anything above 0 is "partial", and 0 is "incorrect".

So the interesting part of each grader is how it computes `score`. Some are simple fractions (a `fill` item scores the share of blanks you got right). Others bend the fraction on purpose, and their comments say why. Free-text formats are harder: find the helper each one uses to compare your text with the expected answer, and read exactly what that helper changes or ignores before comparing.

When you read a grader, ask two questions: what exactly gets counted, and what does the comment say the author was trying to prevent? Then check whether the code really does what the comment claims.

excerpts.quote: function verdictFor(score: number): Verdict { if (score >= 0.999) return "correct"; if (score > 0) return "partial"; return "incorrect"; }

const expected = (item.answer as string[]) ?? []; const detail = expected.map((exp, i) => matchesBlank(response.blanks[i] ?? "", exp)); const hit = detail.filter(Boolean).length; const score = expected.length === 0 ? 0 : hit / expected.length;

items.title: Core idea: FSRS scheduling and the mastery number
items.body:
FSRS is a spaced-repetition scheduler from the `ts-fsrs` library. After each review it updates a card's **stability**; the code comment explains what that number roughly means in days. Note how stability can grow.

Ramp shows a separate **mastery** number from 0 to 1 on its roadmap, built by `cardMastery` in `src/lib/fsrs.ts`. Read the comment above it and then the code, and write the formula down yourself: what each part is, what constants it uses, and what changes once a card is past its due date. The goal, in the author's words, is an honest roadmap.

The rating you get after each answer (1 Again, 2 Hard, 3 Good, 4 Easy) is what FSRS uses to update the card. It is picked by `ratingFor` in `grading.ts`; read its checks in order before predicting a rating. Also find where the scheduler is configured and what each setting there changes.

items.title: Why 'hello' is graded correct against 'Hello'
items.body:
The key is right: graded correct, because `normalizeOutput` lower-cases both sides. `gradePredict` compares the normalised answer with the normalised expected output. The normaliser trims, unifies quotes, collapses whitespace, spaces out commas and colons, drops trailing semicolons, and its last step is `.toLowerCase()`. After that, "hello" and "Hello" are the same string. This tolerance prevents false failures over formatting, but it means a predict item whose whole point is letter case cannot be graded properly.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Partial for a case-only difference**: predict scores are 1 or 0; there is no partial branch.
- **Normalization only touches whitespace, quotes, commas, semicolons**: it also ends with `.toLowerCase()`.
- **Letters compared byte for byte**: they are compared after lower-casing.
